after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
For the function

$$
G(s)=\frac{6}{{s}^{5}},\,s>0
$$

find the inverse Laplace transform of $G(s),$ given that
$L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that we can write $G(s)$ as 

$$
G(s)=\frac{6}{{s}^{5}}=\frac{F(s)}{s},
$$

where $F(s)=\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}.$
Also, we know that

$$
L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{F(s)} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}} \\  & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{3!}{{s}^{3+1}}} \\  & ={t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Additionally, we know that if $L{f(t)}=F(s)$, then

$$
L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{G(s)} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{F(s)}{s}} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}{τ}^{3}\,\text{d}τ \\  & =\frac{{t}^{4}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

For the function G(s)=6s5,s>0 find the inverse Laplace transform of G(s), given that L{tn}=n!sn+1.

a
6t4
b
t520
c
t44
d
t33
e
t3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that we can write G(s) as G(s)=6s5=F(s)s, where F(s)=6s4. Also, we know that L{tn}=n!sn+1. Thus, we get L−1{F(s)}=L−1{6s4}=L−1{3!s3+1}=t3.

Additionally, we know that if L{f(t)}=F(s), then L{∫0tf(τ)dτ}=F(s)s.

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain L−1{G(s)}=L−1{F(s)s}=∫0tf(τ)dτ=∫0tτ3dτ=t44.

For the function G(s)=1s(s+3),s>−3 find the inverse Laplace transform of G(s), given that L{eat}=1s−a, s>a.

a
13(1−e−t)
b
13(e−3t−1)
c
1t+3
d
e−3t
e
13(1−e−3t)
Submit

decision.explanation: Partial fractions give G(s)=(1/3)(1/s-1/(s+3)), so its inverse Laplace transform is (1/3)(1-e^{-3t}). The stated domain has an error: this Laplace transform converges for s>0, not all s>-3.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
For the function

$$
G(s)=\frac{1}{s(s+3)},\,s>-3
$$

find the inverse Laplace transform of $G(s),$ given that
$L{{e}^{at}}=\frac{1}{s-a},\text{ }s>a.$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that we can write $G(s)$ as 

$$
G(s)=\frac{1}{s(s+3)}=\frac{F(s)}{s},
$$

where $F(s)=\frac{1}{s+3}.$
Also, we know that

$$
L{{e}^{at}}=\frac{1}{s-a}.
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{F(s)} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+3}} \\  & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s-(-3)}} \\  & ={e}^{-3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Additionally, we know that if $L{f(t)}=F(s)$, then

$$
L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{G(s)} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{F(s)}{s}} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-3τ}\,\text{d}τ \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3τ}\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(1-{e}^{-3t}).\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Notice that we can write G(s) as G(s)=1s(s+3)=F(s)s, where F(s)=1s+3. Also, we know that L{eat}=1s−a. Thus, we get L−1{F(s)}=L−1{1s+3}=L−1{1s−(−3)}=e−3t.

decision.explanation: The inverse transform of 1/(s²+36) is sin(6t)/6. Dividing by s corresponds to integration from 0 to t, giving ∫₀ᵗ sin(6τ)/6 dτ=(1-cos(6t))/36.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
For the function

$$
G(s)=\frac{1}{s({s}^{2}+36)},\,s>0
$$

find the inverse Laplace transform of $G(s),$ given that
$L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}.$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that we can write $G(s)$ as 

$$
G(s)=\frac{1}{s({s}^{2}+36)}=\frac{F(s)}{s},
$$

where $F(s)=\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+36}.$
Also, we know that

$$
L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}.
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{F(s)} & ={L}^{-1}\,{\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+36}} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\,{\frac{1}{6}\cdot \frac{6}{{s}^{2}+36}} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\,{L}^{-1}\,{\frac{6}{{s}^{2}+{6}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\,sin\,(6t).\end{aligned}
$$

Additionally, we know that if $L{f(t)}=F(s)$, then

$$
L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{G(s)} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{F(s)}{s}} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\frac{1}{6}\,sin\,(6τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & =-\frac{1}{36}cos\,(6τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =\frac{1}{36}(1-cos\,(6t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

For the function G(s)=1s(s2+36),s>0 find the inverse Laplace transform of G(s), given that L{sin⁡(ωt)}=ωs2+ω2.

a
136(1−cos(6t))
b
16sin(6t)
c
136(1−cos⁡(36t))
d
136(1−sin(6t))
e
136cos(6t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that we can write G(s) as G(s)=1s(s2+36)=F(s)s, where F(s)=1s2+36. Also, we know that L{sin⁡(ωt)}=ωs2+ω2. Thus, we get L−1{F(s)}=L−1{1s2+36}=L−1{16⋅6s2+36}=16L−1{6s2+62}=16sin(6t).

Additionally, we know that if L{f(t)}=F(s), then L{∫0tf(τ)dτ}=F(s)s.

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain L−1{G(s)}=L−1{F(s)s}=∫0tf(τ)dτ=∫0t16sin(6τ)dτ=−136cos(6τ)|0t=136(1−cos(6t)).

content.knowledge_point: Finding an Inverse Laplace Transform Using the Integral Rule
content.problem:
For the function

$$
G(s)=\frac{1}{s({s}^{2}+36)},\,s>0
$$

find the inverse Laplace transform of $G(s),$ given that
$L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}.$
content.worked_solution:
Notice that we can write $G(s)$ as 

$$
G(s)=\frac{1}{s({s}^{2}+36)}=\frac{F(s)}{s},
$$

where $F(s)=\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+36}.$
Also, we know that

$$
L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}.
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{F(s)} & ={L}^{-1}\,{\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+36}} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\,{\frac{1}{6}\cdot \frac{6}{{s}^{2}+36}} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\,{L}^{-1}\,{\frac{6}{{s}^{2}+{6}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\,sin\,(6t).\end{aligned}
$$

Additionally, we know that if $L{f(t)}=F(s)$, then

$$
L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{G(s)} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{F(s)}{s}} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\frac{1}{6}\,sin\,(6τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & =-\frac{1}{36}cos\,(6τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =\frac{1}{36}(1-cos\,(6t)).\end{aligned}
$$

before.name: Question 4
before.problem:
Suppose we wish to find $L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ}$ given $L{f(t)}=F(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ={{field-1}}\,{|}_{0}^{t}=A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ}=L{A(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & ⇒ & du={A}^{′}(t)\text{ }dt \\ dv={{field-3}} & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }({{field-4}}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=$ {{field-5}}, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-6}}\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$
before.worked_solution:
Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ & =A(τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =A(t)-A(0) \\  & =A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ} & =L{A(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & \,⇒\, & du={A}^{′}(t)\,dt \\ dv={e}^{-st}\,dt & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A(0)=0$ and $\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ we have $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=0$ and

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{1}{s}\cdot F(s) \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Let A(t) be the anti-derivative of f(t) such that A′(t)=f(t) and A(0)=0. Then, ∫0tf(τ)dτ=A(τ)|0t=A(t)−A(0)=A(t).

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

L{∫0tf(τ)dτ}=L{A(t)}=∫0∞e−stA(t)dt.

Now, let's use integration by parts: u=A(t)⇒du=A′(t)dtdv=e−stdt⇒v=−1se−st

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get ∫0∞e−stA(t)dt=A(t)(−1se−st)|0∞−∫0∞(−1se−st)A′(t)dt.

Since A(0)=0 and 1se−st→0 as t→∞, we have −1sA(t)e−st|0∞=0 and ∫0∞e−stA(t)dt=1s∫0∞e−stA′(t)dt.

Finally, using that A′(t)=f(t), we obtain 1s∫0∞e−stA′(t)dt=1s∫0∞e−stf(t)dt=1s⋅F(s)=F(s)s.

decision.explanation: Use A(τ) as the antiderivative and e^{-st} as the Laplace kernel. Integration by parts gives v=-e^{-st}/s and a zero boundary term in the convergence region s>max(s₀,0). Finally, e^{-st}A′(t)=e^{-st}f(t), so the result is F(s)/s.

observation.problem:
Suppose we wish to find $L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ}$ given $L{f(t)}=F(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ={{field-1}}\,{|}_{0}^{t}=A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ}=L{A(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

observation.problem:
Suppose we wish to find $L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ}$ given $L{f(t)}=F(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ={{field-1}}\,{|}_{0}^{t}=A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ}=L{A(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & ⇒ & du={A}^{′}(t)\text{ }dt \\ dv={{field-3}} & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

observation.problem:
Suppose we wish to find $L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ}$ given $L{f(t)}=F(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ={{field-1}}\,{|}_{0}^{t}=A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ}=L{A(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & ⇒ & du={A}^{′}(t)\text{ }dt \\ dv={{field-3}} & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }({{field-4}}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

observation.problem:
Suppose we wish to find $L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ}$ given $L{f(t)}=F(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ={{field-1}}\,{|}_{0}^{t}=A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ}=L{A(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & ⇒ & du={A}^{′}(t)\text{ }dt \\ dv={{field-3}} & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }({{field-4}}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=$ {{field-5}}, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

observation.problem:
Suppose we wish to find $L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ}$ given $L{f(t)}=F(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ={{field-1}}\,{|}_{0}^{t}=A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ}=L{A(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & ⇒ & du={A}^{′}(t)\text{ }dt \\ dv={{field-3}} & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }({{field-4}}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=$ {{field-5}}, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-6}}\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

observation.name: Question 4
observation.problem:
Suppose we wish to find $L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ}$ given $L{f(t)}=F(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ={{field-1}}\,{|}_{0}^{t}=A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ}=L{A(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & ⇒ & du={A}^{′}(t)\text{ }dt \\ dv={{field-3}} & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }({{field-4}}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=$ {{field-5}}, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-6}}\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$
observation.worked_solution:
Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ & =A(τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =A(t)-A(0) \\  & =A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ} & =L{A(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & \,⇒\, & du={A}^{′}(t)\,dt \\ dv={e}^{-st}\,dt & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A(0)=0$ and $\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ we have $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=0$ and

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{1}{s}\cdot F(s) \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Let A(t) be the anti-derivative of f(t) such that A′(t)=f(t) and A(0)=0. Then, ∫0tf(τ)dτ=A(τ)|0t=A(t)−A(0)=A(t).

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

L{∫0tf(τ)dτ}=L{A(t)}=∫0∞e−stA(t)dt.

Now, let's use integration by parts: u=A(t)⇒du=A′(t)dtdv=e−stdt⇒v=−1se−st

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get ∫0∞e−stA(t)dt=A(t)(−1se−st)|0∞−∫0∞(−1se−st)A′(t)dt.

Since A(0)=0 and 1se−st→0 as t→∞, we have −1sA(t)e−st|0∞=0 and ∫0∞e−stA(t)dt=1s∫0∞e−stA′(t)dt.

Finally, using that A′(t)=f(t), we obtain 1s∫0∞e−stA′(t)dt=1s∫0∞e−stf(t)dt=1s⋅F(s)=F(s)s.

decision.explanation: Use A(τ) as the antiderivative and e^{-st} as the Laplace kernel. Integration by parts gives v=-e^{-st}/s and a zero boundary term in the convergence region s>max(s₀,0). Finally, e^{-st}A′(t)=e^{-st}f(t), so the result is F(s)/s.

after.problem:
Suppose we wish to find $L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ}$ given $L{f(t)}=F(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ={{field-1}}\,{|}_{0}^{t}=A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ}=L{A(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & ⇒ & du={A}^{′}(t)\text{ }dt \\ dv={{field-3}} & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }({{field-4}}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=$ {{field-5}}, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-6}}\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ & =A(τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =A(t)-A(0) \\  & =A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ} & =L{A(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & \,⇒\, & du={A}^{′}(t)\,dt \\ dv={e}^{-st}\,dt & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A(0)=0$ and $\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ we have $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=0$ and

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{1}{s}\cdot F(s) \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let A(t) be the anti-derivative of f(t) such that A′(t)=f(t) and A(0)=0. Then, ∫0tf(τ)dτ=A(τ)|0t=A(t)−A(0)=A(t).

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

L{∫0tf(τ)dτ}=L{A(t)}=∫0∞e−stA(t)dt.

Now, let's use integration by parts: u=A(t)⇒du=A′(t)dtdv=e−stdt⇒v=−1se−st

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get ∫0∞e−stA(t)dt=A(t)(−1se−st)|0∞−∫0∞(−1se−st)A′(t)dt.

Since A(0)=0 and 1se−st→0 as t→∞, we have −1sA(t)e−st|0∞=0 and ∫0∞e−stA(t)dt=1s∫0∞e−stA′(t)dt.

Finally, using that A′(t)=f(t), we obtain 1s∫0∞e−stA′(t)dt=1s∫0∞e−stf(t)dt=1s⋅F(s)=F(s)s.

content.problem:
Suppose we wish to find $L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ}$ given $L{f(t)}=F(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ={{field-1}}\,{|}_{0}^{t}=A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ}=L{A(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & ⇒ & du={A}^{′}(t)\text{ }dt \\ dv={{field-3}} & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }({{field-4}}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=$ {{field-5}}, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-6}}\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$
content.worked_solution:
Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ & =A(τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =A(t)-A(0) \\  & =A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ} & =L{A(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & \,⇒\, & du={A}^{′}(t)\,dt \\ dv={e}^{-st}\,dt & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A(0)=0$ and $\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ we have $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=0$ and

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{1}{s}\cdot F(s) \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$
